# 1 History of the Method

The term,[^1] pragmatism,[^2] is derived from the same Greek word [pi rho alpha gamma mu alpha], meaning action, from which our words 'practice' and 'practical' come.[^3] It was first introduced into philosophy by Mr. Charles Peirce in 1878.[^4] Mr. Peirce, after pointing out that our beliefs are really rules for action, said that to develope a thought's meaning, we need only determine what conduct it is fitted to produce: that conduct is for us its sole significance.[^5] And the tangible fact at the root of all our thought-distinctions, however subtle, is that there is no one of them so fine as to consist in anything but a possible difference of practice.[^6] To attain perfect clearness in our thoughts of an object, then, we need only consider what conceivable effects of a practical kind the object may involve--what sensations we are to expect from it, and what reactions we must prepare.[^7] Our conception of these effects, whether immediate or remote, is then for us the whole of our conception of the object, so far as that conception has positive significance at all.[^8]

This is the principle of Peirce, the principle of pragmatism.[^9] The word 'pragmatism' spread, and at present it fairly spots the pages of the philosophic journals.[^10] It is evident that the term applies itself conveniently to a number of tendencies that hitherto have lacked a collective name, and that it has 'come to stay.'[^11]

To take in the importance of Peirce's principle, one must get accustomed to applying it to concrete cases.[^12] Ostwald, the illustrious Leipzig chemist, had been making perfectly distinct use of the principle of pragmatism in his lectures on the philosophy of science, tho he had not called it by that name.[^13]

"All realities influence our practice," he wrote,[^14] "and that influence is their meaning for us.[^15] I am accustomed to put questions to my classes in this way: In what respects would the world be different if this alternative or that were true?[^16] If I can find nothing that would become different, then the alternative has no sense."[^17]

That is, the rival views mean practically the same thing, and meaning, other than practical, there is for us none.[^18]

It is astonishing to see how many philosophical disputes collapse into insignificance the moment you subject them to this simple test of tracing a concrete consequence.[^19] There can BE no difference any-where that doesn't MAKE a difference elsewhere--no difference in abstract truth that doesn't express itself in a difference in concrete fact and in conduct consequent upon that fact, imposed on somebody, somehow, somewhere and somewhen.[^20] The whole function of philosophy ought to be to find out what definite difference it will make to you and me, at definite instants of our life, if this world-formula or that world-formula be the true one.[^21]

There is absolutely nothing new in the pragmatic method,[^22] a method of settling metaphysical disputes that otherwise might be interminable.[^23] Socrates was an adept at it.[^24] Aristotle used it methodically.[^25] Locke, Berkeley and Hume made momentous contributions to truth by its means.[^26] Shadworth Hodgson keeps insisting that realities are only what they are 'known-as.'[^27] But these forerunners of pragmatism used it in fragments: they were preluders only.[^28] Not until in our time has it generalized itself, become conscious of a universal mission, pretended to a conquering destiny.[^29]
